new:
Case shows a noun's role in the sentence, so a Russian sentence relies less on word order than an English one. Compare Собаки ненавидят котов. — Dogs hate cats. with Коты ненавидят собак. — Cats hate dogs.

The accusative marks the direct object. Feminine nouns change the ending -а to -у and the ending -я to -ю; feminine nouns ending in the soft sign -ь do not change.

Masculine nouns follow animacy. An inanimate noun keeps its nominative form: Я де́лал стул. — I made a chair. An animate noun takes the same form as its genitive: Я люблю этого кота. — I like this cat. The form matches the genitive, but the noun is still the direct object.

Object pronouns: Я — I, Меня — me. Мы — we, Нас — us. Ты — you, Тебя — you. Вы — you, Вас — you. Он — he, Его — him. Она — she, Её — her. Они — they, Их — them.

With the accusative, в means to or into, and на means onto or toward: Я шёл в дом — I walked into the house. Я шёл на улицу — I walked onto the street.

With the prepositional case, в means in or at, and на means upon or at: Я жил в Лондоне — I lived in London. Оно на столе — It's on the table.

The accusative shows direction; the prepositional shows location.

в and на with the accusative for direction and the prepositional for location.

Possessives such as Мой, Твой, Наш and Ваш act like adjectives: they change to match the noun they describe, not the owner. Твой is the informal or singular your; Ваш is the formal or plural your.

In the accusative, my has the forms Мой and Моего (masculine, inanimate and animate), мою (feminine), Моё (neuter), and Мои and Моих (plural, inanimate and animate). Our follows the same pattern: Наш, Нашего, нашу, Наше, Наши, Наших.

The third-person possessives его (his), её (her) and их (their) do not change with the noun they describe: Я хочу его кота — I want his cat. Я хочу его котов — I want his cats.

Masculine nouns add -ы: стол — table, столы — tables. Feminine nouns ending in -а replace it with -ы: машина — car, машины — cars. Feminine nouns ending in -я or -ь take -и. Neuter nouns ending in -о take -а: письмо — letter, письма — letters.

Prepositions that take the genitive: Для — for; У — by, near; Без — without; Из — from, out of; От — away from. Я хочу́ пода́рок для моего́ дру́га — I want a present for my friend. Ко́фе без молока́ — Black coffee. Я из А́нглии — I'm from England.

Genitive adjectives: masculine and neuter -ого (-его after a hushing consonant), feminine -ой (-ей), plural -ых (-их): Кило́ хоро́шего ру́сского сы́ра — A kilogram of good Russian cheese. To say someone has something, put the owner in the genitive after у and follow it with есть and the thing owned in the nominative: У вас есть сын? — Do you have a son? Да, у меня есть сын. — Yes, I have a son. У твоего́ му́жа есть оди́н друг — Your husband has one friend.

To say that something is absent, use нет followed by the genitive: Нет рестора́нов — There are no restaurants. В Москве́ нет ста́рых зда́ний — There are no old buildings in Moscow. У меня́ нет сы́на — I don't have a son. У моего́ бра́та нет де́нег — My brother doesn't have any money.
